title: Boyhood playground, the French Market and helping the vendors
summary: Albert recalls the oak trees, the circle, horse-and-buggy days and the old market, where he helped vendors for an apple or orange and fetched his father.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Okay. Anyway, you know, those houses and everything, to me, everything is beautiful except for what they've done to play banana.

That really, you know, that's one of the dreams of my my boyhood days. I remember those great big massive acorn trees. Well, they're old trees. We called them acorn trees. And those were beautiful days for us to play. It was a playground for the poor Negro kids, which I am. And I look at that experience and gee whiz, what a change. There used to be a circle up there on the sand and all in Clevemont. We used to call it the circle. And it was a big palm tree going into this thing. And it all sat around on this cement circle. I didn't sit there until time to go home and exchange stores. But all all of that is gone. Were there a lot of

No cars. Cars were almost a thing in the past. They were just beginning to come in. I'm going back to the horse and the buggy days. Because the salmon oil market is now what the circle market is. Well, there's as much difference in that market there and the market that I'm referring to as daylight and darkness. This is a modern superstore as they call it. And the salmon oil market, the butchers had their stalls. And the vegetable vendors had their stalls. And the fish vendors had their their section set aside for that. And the same token, the poultry people. Each individual had his own. And on the outside of the market was a baby old water trough where the horses used to come to drink. Well, we'd wait until the fresh water come in before the horses got there. And we'd be working around, the kids working around and helping the people get their stands up and get to drink before the horse leaves. Yeah. Yeah. Well,
